438: \subsubsection{The SFR Formula}
439: 
440: To convert $\Sigma_{H\alpha}$ in units of ergs s$^{-1}$ pc$^{-2}$, as shown in
441: Figures \ref{fig-n801sb} and \ref{fig-u2885sb}, to SFR in units of M\solar\
442: yr$^{-1}$ kpc$^{-2}$, we begin with the formula of Kennicutt (1998): ${\rm
443: SFR}_{H\alpha} {\rm (M\solar\ yr^{-1})} = 7.9\times10^{-42} L_{H\alpha} {\rm (ergs ~
444: s^{-1})}$. We multiply the \ha\ surface density by 0.82 to remove [NII] and then
445: adjust the formula for the deviation of the metallicity from solar, the abundance
446: that Kennicutt used. For the latter, we use the synthesis models of STARBURST99
447: (Leitherer \et\ 1999), with constant SFR and a Salpeter (1955) stellar initial mass
448: function. Their Figure 78, which gives the number of photons below 912 \AA, enables
449: us to find the average flux of ionizing photons per second from a stellar population
450: relative to that at solar and so to modify Kennicutt's \ha\ formula as a function of
451: $Z$ from twice solar to below solar. 
452: The correction factor at twice solar metallicity is 1.18 and at 40\% solar is 0.87. 
453: We interpolate to determine the correction factor for the metallicity at a given radius.
454: The derived SFRs for NGC 801 and UGC 2885 are shown in Figure \ref{fig-sfr}. 
455: 
456: Integrated SFRs use the oxygen abundance at the
457: half-light radius to determine the SFR formula. For both galaxies this is approximately
458: $z=0.03$. Thus, the SFRs need to be multiplied by a factor of 1.089 to adjust
459: for the metallicity.
460: The integrated SFRs are given in Table \ref{tab-gal}.
461: 
462: We have also computed a SFR necessary to form the stellar mass that currently exists
463: in each galaxy, SFR$_V$. For this we used the $V$-band surface brightness to
464: determine the mass in stars and assume a timescale of 12 Gyr for the formation of
465: that stellar mass. We obtain $M/L_V$ as a function of (B$-$V)$_0$ from Bell \& de
466: Jong (2001). If the uncertainty in the color is  greater than 0.1 mag, we use the
467: average  (B$-$V)$_0$ in the outer disk. SFR$_V$ is the SFR necessary to produce the
468: original mass in stars. Because the $M/L_V$ yields the mass currently in stars, we
469: correct this by a factor of two for the mass recycled back into the interstellar
470: medium (Brinchmann \et\ 2004) in order to use the total mass ever formed into stars
471: in computing the lifetime average ${\rm SFR}_V$. The ratio ${\rm SFR}_{H\alpha}/{\rm
472: SFR}_V$ is shown in Figure \ref{fig-rat}. We also compute the current surface
473: density of the stellar mass $\Sigma_*$ in units of M\solar\ pc$^{-2}$.

1013: taking place in regions of locally higher gas densities, namely, spiral arms.
1014: The traditional Toomre (1964) gravitational instability parameter $Q$ is everywhere larger than 1, implying a stable gas.
1015: However, when we include the
1016: stellar disk thickness with dissipative gas and both radial and azimuthal forcing ($Q_{eff}$), the outer regions become
1017: marginally unstable to form spiral arms. Star formation occurs in these arms with higher local densities than the surrounding average.
1018: Generally spirals grow at higher $Q$ than the radial stability threshold, so the spirals are the primary instability,
1019: from which star formation follows at the locally increased densities in the arms.
1020: 
1021: We have traced smooth exponential stellar disks over 3-orders of magnitude and 4-6 disk scale lengths,
1022: in spite of a highly variable gravitational instability parameter. Thus, gravitational instability thresholds
1023: do not seem relevant to the stellar disk.
1024: One possibility for creating an exponential disk is that
1025: the star formation activity has an exponential profile and this forces the stellar disk to build up such a profile too.
1026: Another possibility is that the stellar disk is continuously adjusted to an exponential shape regardless of the star formation profile.
1027: The latter could be due to global dynamical processes that scatter the stars.
1028: However, the known scattering processes only operate in spiral systems and cannot explain the same situation of smooth exponential
1029: disks observed in \dirr\ galaxies.
1030: Perhaps clumps in \dirr\ galaxies play the role of scattering centers to make the disks exponential (Hunter \et\ 2011).
